Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified error margin for MCM results. Our proposed ILP models for various MCM configurations are available in an open-source tool, integrated with the FloPoCo VHDL code generator, providing a complete flow from coefficients to hardware design. Thorough experiments were conducted to assess the models, followed by a detailed analysis of how design metrics impact actual hardware implementation.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research from multiple viewpoints, followed by a discussion of prospective future directions and practical applications.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in 
high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, where significant progress has been 
made over the past decade in advancing the field. This progress could soon lead 
to upgraded existing facilities, enhancements to facilities still under 
construction (such as PIP-II), well-established proposals, or newly emerging 
ideas like the FCC-ee and future proton intensity upgrade at Fermilab, among 
others. Innovations in RF technology not only contribute to HEP but also extend 
beyond to fields such as nuclear physics, basic energy sciences, and other areas, 
as evidenced by European XFEL, LCLS-II and related facilities, or SHINE, 
EIC, and FRIB. Therefore, an extensive R&D program focusing on RF technology 
is needed to tackle challenges in accelerator-based applications and introduce 
new, promising technologies.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments.

Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC). This innovative architecture is designed for cloud computing scenarios, specifically incorporating a novel type of CPU accumulator that is fully compliant with the Advanced RISC Machine (ARM) Instruction Set. Furthermore, VSP incorporates a novel zero-knowledge proof system tailored for arm64 architecture, including support for 64-bit instructions and floating point operations. To evaluate the performance of VSP, it is surrounded by a comprehensive toolchain consisting of a C compilation framework and a Linux operating system, all of which are developed from the ground up as zero-knowledge proofs to facilitate comparative studies with existing solutions. This toolchain, referred to as the VSP Linux, boasts an impressive level of functionality, including support for memory management with GCC and Metacommands. To assess its efficiency, VSP implements a hands-on approach, starting with benchmarking software and hardware, followed by a detailed evaluation of the entire system.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear projection matrices in self-attention for accurate parsing. Consequently, the unsupervised models were transformed into few-shot parsing models, FPOA and FPIO, to learn better parsing matrices with limited annotated trees. On the Penn Treebank dataset, the unsupervised model UPIO achieved parsing results on a par with current best techniques on short sentences. Meanwhile, the few-shot parsing model FPIO surpassed previous comparable models, trained on only twenty trees instead of fifty. Importantly, both models showed superior cross-lingual parsing capabilities on SPMRL languages, outperforming earlier methods on most of these languages.

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application, specifically employing hyperspectral images for cityscape object segmentation using an unsupervised learning approach that circumvents the need for manual object classification. This method capitalizes on the rich spectral data inherent in HSI images, which facilitates efficient object segmentation within complex urban environments. By analyzing the inherent properties of HSI images and developing a corresponding segmentation framework, we demonstrate how these images can improve low-quality labels, ultimately leading to higher accuracy in object segmentation. Our results demonstrate that this technique produces competitive results and outperforms manually refined labels in certain scenarios. Moreover, the refined labels derived from HSI images contribute significantly to the enhancement of object segmentation when combined with existing methods. This research successfully verifies the potential of HSI images in advanced visual applications, paving the way for potential future developments in computer vision.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation rate is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to conventional theories. Additionally, we apply spectroscopic analysis to determine the surface abundance of chemical elements. Our results show relatively high iron and silicates' abundance compared to the sun's values, likely a result of dusty winds that interacted with circumstellar material. We also determine the angular momentum evolution of the star and compare it with universal time and velocity markers. Furthermore, we investigate possible explanations for the unusual internal rotation pattern of this star, suggesting an alternative scenario where a massive inner core may exist with a distinct and slower rotation rate.

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST, which cannot be achieved with the traditional RAM model under established assumptions. The proven properties of this new model, termed the CRAM, are based on the inherent limitations of the previous RAM model and are attributed to the fundamental properties of the model itself. Additionally, the CRAM model incorporates desirable features from various widely used computation models.

To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets.

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters.

We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, correlations within one-dimensional systems have yet to be considered as a factor in topological structure. Research has shown that in one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems, local correlations can destroy topological characteristics, even in the absence of disorder. We developed an extended version of the correlation function approach that applies to non-Hermitian systems and discovered that under certain conditions, correlations can give rise to a topological index distinct from the non-Hermitian skin effect parameter. We demonstrated this through studies of simple models and found that in certain cases, all eigenstates contribute equally to the corner occupancy, thereby yielding an indeterminate correlation topological number. Furthermore, a related bulk correlation function can serve as a precursor indicator of the non-Hermitian skin effect. Our research reveals the significant role correlations play in shaping the topological structure of one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems and offers a valuable tool for analyzing the non-Hermitian skin effect in higher-dimensional systems.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the consideration of tested non-standard interactions.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By integrating various techniques to extract changes from the images, it significantly outperformed current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised change detection across diverse datasets.

Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of squares and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a subset of natural numbers such that when you combine these two sets with addition, the result encompasses all natural numbers greater than or equal to some finite number $N_0$. Now, the $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ denotes the count of all possible pairs of $s$ from $\mathcal{S}$ and $w$ from $\mathcal{W}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Previous studies, such as those by Chen and Fang, have shown that the total count of these pairs minus the total natural numbers up to $N$ exceeds $N^{1/4}$ multiplied by the natural logarithm of $N$. Here, a refined version of that finding is provided with a revised lower bound of $N^{1/3}$.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which is not entirely under one's control.
A method involving coherent perturbation through microwave engineering in conjunction with optical detection offers a highly sensitive means of identifying individual atoms' influence even when their presence is masked by energy gaps due to the exchange of photons. 
This method has the capability to execute complex operations on atoms simultaneously, and it has been demonstrated that the efficient conversion of spin-valley states into a forbidden band is feasible in high-quality silicon material.
Additionally, valley magnetic moments can be addressed independently, and it has been shown that the combination of light manipulation and electronic engineering can be utilized to control the interaction between valleys and spins.
This technique holds great potential for the development of scalable silicon quantum processors in which valley and spin degrees of freedom control and manipulation can be efficiently accomplished.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical applications. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently implementing and prototyping nature-inspired optimization algorithms. By integrating 15 established techniques and 112 benchmark functions, as well as supporting 11 novel hypercomplex-based approaches, our framework surpasses others in its domain, thus marking it as a groundbreaking innovation in optimization software development. Utilizing LibOPT under the C paradigm proves to be remarkably user-friendly and adaptable, as evidenced by the inclusion of clear source-code examples demonstrating the practical usage of benchmark functions.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space symmetries represented by a four-momentum group. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect assumptions and lack success. We demonstrate that momentum exchange underlies a relativistic covariance principle in the braiding of quantum numbers, solving a persistent challenge in the field.

We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of wide bandgap semiconductors. We utilize this technique to
investigate charge transport in scCVD diamond by exciting its charge carriers
with a femtosecond laser. Due to its two-photon nature, the technique confines
charge carrier generation in 3-D around the laser focal point. This localized
charge injection enables us to study the semiconductor bulk with high 3-D
resolution. We mapped the diamond's bulk electrical field at varying depths by
taking advantage of charge spatial confinement. The results were then compared
to X-ray diffraction topological field measurements. The approach allows us to
investigate charge transport in semiconductor materials with high spatial
resolution, which is particularly valuable for studying diamond and GaN bulk
semiconductors.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieved top-tier outcomes, securing first, second, and third place in both the misogyny identification and classification tasks.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation.

Several network communication scenarios begin with a central distribution point where information is transmitted to a group of clients through a limited distribution channel. As a result, a reliable communication method called centralized coded caching aims to ensure seamless data exchange. A key caching method involves breaking down information into multiple parts and storing them in a distributed manner. These cached fragments are then drawn upon in a data recovery process which ensures the seamless data exchange. A specific caching scheme, the Vector Cache (VC), was introduced in 2018 and demonstrated optimal performance. However, the VC method came with a challenge of significant computational complexity. A major advancement was introduced by Msellouf and Radani in 2020, presenting a new model based on VC, with the aim of achieving optimal performance at a reduced computational cost. This new model is examined and a successful reduction in computational complexity is achieved, resulting in a new model with a linear computational complex and optimal performance.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations, and build upon this base with control techniques and efficient state sampling methods to develop practical nonlinear gates, especially a nonlinear Hadamard gate. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing redefines the paradigm by incorporating principles from nonlinear quantum mechanics, effectively applying it to interferometry and information processing.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show a clear increase above a binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ fit, and their transverse momentum spectra follow a similar trend as Au$+$Au collisions, involving a similar number of participants. We have determined the inverse slopes of the photon spectra and compared them to hadronic and electromagnetic measurements in $p$$+$$p$ and other central heavy ion collisions. Moreover, we found that the photon spectra in Cu$+$Cu collisions exhibit a similar dependence on charged particle multiplicity as Au$+$Au collisions, obtained from the same run at the same centre of mass energy.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum allowed edge density in a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph. Our study focuses on understanding the structure of K4^3-free hypergraphs and providing new upper bounds for the edge density. We introduce a new concept called codegree squared sum, denoted as d2(G), representing the total squared weight of codegrees in a 3-uniform hypergraph G. Our main result shows that any K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph has a codegree squared sum of at most 120n. We then demonstrate that this upper bound is nearly precise, as well as show that our techniques can also be applied to solve other related problems, such as determining the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph over specific discrete sets of vertices and edges.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of traditional anti-aling methods make them more of a hindrance than a help in this context. This is because they undermine the vector nature of the maps by treating each path stroke as a pixel-based image, necessitating an unnecessary conversion and subsequent rendering of each stroke. In contrast, a more tailored approach would involve directly applying anti-aling principles to the map's B-spline curves, thereby bypassing the need for a costly image transformation. This not only enables faster rendering but also enables more precise control over curve rendering quality. In this study, a novel anti-aling algorithm utilizing the map's B-spline curves is proposed. This approach starts by approximating the line joins as B-spline curves and then applies a series of transformations to generate an anti-aling mask. A series of test lines is then used to determine the optimal rendering points, after which the resulting points are passed through a smoothing process and finally rendered using the device's B-spline curve capabilities. In comparison to traditional anti-aling methods, this approach yields superior results in terms of visual experience and system performance. Furthermore, this study also proposes two optimization techniques for reducing the number of rendering points while minimizing visual distortion. The results show that these techniques not only reduce the memory overhead but also yield a significant speed increase. The proposed algorithm and optimization techniques are implemented in the Ark

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications on the puzzles of excess positrons and the widespread TeV gamma-ray excess. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues based on the anticipation of discovering more pulsar halos and carrying out deeper investigations into the brightest sources.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have explored the use of data-driven soft grippers' dynamics models. However, these models often rely on high-dimensional soft grippers' state-space representations, which necessitate dimensionality reduction to facilitate control design. In this paper, we introduce the Soft Gripper Model Predictive Control (SGMPC) approach, combining iterative methods to compactly represent the dynamics with MPC. The SGMPC's strength lies in its multi-step optimization solution, which uses predictive filtering to address the non-linearity and connection between the soft grippers' dynamics. The proposed method outperforms current approaches in simulation studies and demonstrates promising results in real-world experiments, successfully reducing the dimensionality by two orders of magnitude while achieving superior performance compared to existing control strategies.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies should make up a significant portion of these distant galaxy populations. This study uses a highly detailed analysis of data collected from multiple observations of a particularly old and distant galaxy called J2102+6015. High-resolution imaging of J2102+6015's energy emissions, which were captured through a highly precise technique called VLBI at a wavelength of 8.4 GHz, revealed two distinct energy-producing regions. This imaging revealed two distinct energy-producing regions aligned east to west that displayed flat or reversed spectra. Importantly, the separation between these regions has changed very little over a 13 year period. Consequently, the speed at which the energy regions move is thought to be less than about 0.04 arc-seconds per year. In addition, our detailed analysis indicates that J2102+6015 is very likely a younger, dense and symmetric structure rather than the core of a highly energetic active galaxy as had been suggested by earlier studies.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might enable the detection of supermassive binary black holes. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to identify gravitational wave memory and provides an opportunity to advance our understanding of gravity theory.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe underwent a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples in space time that scientists could detect. Developing models where this phase transition happens and analyzing the sound waves that traverse the split phase and their interaction with cosmic ripples is a crucial area of study. These sound waves can take on properties similar to those of gravitational waves, with characteristics that differentiate them from traditional predictions; our current understanding indicates these sounds waves can have frequencies in the range of 10 to 100 Hz when they reach us.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility values between communication nodes. This language enhances the vocabulary for message transmission by splitting complex data into simpler components and allows for generalization to unforeseen scenarios. A neural network model is used to reconstruct causal states based on the relevant data attributes at the transmitter, which are then evaluated by a receiver that implements a symbolic logical formula execution using AI components. Specifically, this implementation leverages the Generative Flow Networks tool for improved semantic reliability. This communication system has been designed to evaluate a new set of metrics, such as semantic information and distortion, using rigorous category theory algebraic properties, expanding beyond traditional notions of uncertainty as defined by Shannon. Simulation results demonstrate the system's capability to transmit data more efficiently and with enhanced reliability compared to conventional wireless systems. This research proposes a new, comprehensive approach to evaluating communication systems that incorporate uncharted information and causal reasoning.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can be computationally demanding, hindering their feasibility in certain scenarios, continuous advancements in technology and mathematical modeling enable the development of faster, more accurate systems. A hybrid word suggestion model proposed here, combining elements of Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis and considering context provided by surrounding words in the sentence, demonstrates considerable promise. Notably, this model achieved a 44.2% accuracy rating in the MSR Sentence Completion Challenge.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in re-ranking. Experimental results demonstrate a considerable enhancement over the baseline on metrics such as Recall, MRR, and Click-Through-Rate in an online setting, and we further observed improvements when applied to STAMP and NARM models on two public real-world datasets for the task of next-click prediction.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in a finite permeability block, while the second examines flow and transport through a large anisotropic anisotropic volume with a significant fracture network.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly eliminate disturbances, thus minimizing the time required for the swarm to reach its destination and consequently lowering the energy consumption associated with this process. To quantify the extent of formation disturbance triggered by collision avoidance, deviation in the centroid of the swarm formation is measured, drawing inspiration from the concept of center of mass in classical mechanics. The study's experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of the proposed technique in terms of performance and energy efficiency.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a maximum multiplicity of two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users in specific regions. However, RSUs are limited to specific areas due to infrastructure constraints, leading to the use of mobile vehicle relays for expanded coverage. Yet, relying on these relays may place net users in certain situations, increasing the risk of coercion and related threats. To mitigate potential risks, we develop an asynchronous FL-based cooperative detection system allowing vehicles in various locations to jointly detect potential hazards without compromising privacy. Vehicles in each area form local datasets, with each vehicle contributing encrypted information to a common aggregator. A trusted but untrusted authority provides securely shared random coefficients for each relay and supports secure, decentralized training of the detection model across all vehicles. By incorporating the challenges posed by partial observability and the need for cooperative detection, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our system in addressing net users' concerns and maintaining privacy while detecting potential hazards.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as editors.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and providing explicit, continuous-trace algebra computations for the resulting non-trivial Dixmier-Douady classes. Ultimately, we demonstrate that any solvmanifold can be represented as a $C^*$-algebra bundle of noncommutative tori, which we explicitly compute, while the monodromy of the original torus bundle is translated into a Morita equivalence among fiber algebras.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces the complexity of PAC code decoding. By replacing the Euclidean metric with our proposed function, we demonstrate the results of eight-year old PAC code architectures reaching the performance of PAC codes decoded using the maximum likelihood metric, which was a goal first outlined by Lu and Feng in 2015. Our proposed metric function maintains the property of being Euclidean and orthogonality properties, which simplifies the decoding process. Additionally, simulations have shown that our method achieves optimal error rate performance for higher signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) with a simpler decoder structure.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, to resolve ambiguity caused by occlusions, our system adopts joint optimization for both hands and objects. In our training process, our system only uses synthetic, constantly changing object and hand pairs for a robust generalization. In our experiments, our method outperformed other state-of-the-art hand tracking methods on real world records and succeeded in tracking hands and objects in difficult scenarios such as when they are completely hidden or moving too fast.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize a characterizing model for a rotationally symmetric object's pose, eliminating the need for complex mathematical formulations. The model's robustness is enhanced through a robust optimization process that efficiently and robustly estimates object and camera poses from a small number of key frames. The benefits of our system include its flexibility, adaptability, and ability to operate in various real-world scenarios without the need for a controlled environment. The integration of a camera model based object localization scheme allows us to pose the problem as a factor graph, solving for object and camera positions, orientations, and scales. The proposed system is validated on a camera and a rotating plastic bowl, with promising results. The related code is publicly available on GitHub.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We develop test statistics that analyze the behavior of all units within a study, either by considering the treatment status of surrounding units (K-neighborhood) or by utilizing the last treated unit affecting the target unit (L-last). Our results show the existing statistical tests, tailored to specific units, are ineffective against the given types of interference, while our methods demonstrate strong power in detecting interferences up to half the size of the given K-neighborhood.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which may equal and potentially surpass those produced by the star's nuclear reactions early on. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's volume and persist throughout the star's lifetime. This information is then used to assess potential impacts of this process on the cooling of a star in the context of existing constraints on dark matter particles.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers 1250 square degrees of the sky, equating to 12 billion solar masses of weak-lensing data. A total of 27 million galaxies were analyzed, with 4.5 million deemed suitable for shear calibration. This collaboration has yielded groundbreaking findings, as the additive and residual multiplicative shear biases were successfully eliminated, meeting the requirements of Planck Component Separation findings. By strategically targeting specific galaxy populations, the projects' cataloging also encompasses diverse galaxy classes, facilitating research in the areas of galaxy evolution and assembly. The UNIONS project's catalog is set to streamline future surveys such as LSST, incorporating an unprecedented 16 million weak-lensing clusters of galaxies, covering an area of 30,000 square degrees and possessing exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds. The projects' catalog is set to streamline future surveys such as the LSST, incorporating an unprecedented 16 million weak-lensing clusters of galaxies, covering an area of 30,000 square degrees and possessing exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from the rotation sequence for no integer $m$, then, as $N$ approaches infinity, the parity of the sizes of sets consisting of numbers of the form $\{q\alpha\}$ within the interval $[0,b)$ that correspond to $q$ values up to $N$ displays evenly distributed occurrences.

In the case where $\alpha$ is equal to $\sqrt{d}$, an algebraically independent number of magnitude, the finding presents an innovation on a result from Veech's work with V. Sprindzuk. Also, when $\alpha$ is equal to $\zeta e^{i\pi/3}$, with $\zeta$ being a complex number whose argument is irrationally related to $\pi/3$, the conclusion represents an advancement of a finding in a paper published by J. V\"{o}lkel, M. Ziegler, S. Tchepelov, M. K\"{o}hler, and S. Haase.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions as well as long-range order. Finite-size scaling of the spin stiffness based on our in-plane theory shows a perfect match between theoretical and experimental critical temperatures, clearly indicating that the complex magnetic phase diagram of [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 is determined by field-induced XY anisotropy and concomitant BKT physics.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z-rotation gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. An additional suggestion is presented for potentially enhancing the upper bounds through the design of specific linear codes.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and considering 
fractional energy density restrictions, which can help determine real universe scenarios.
We will analyze the effects of spatial curvature and initial conditions on fractional 
energy density to determine the viability of real universe scenarios in the non-interacting 
case. Furthermore, in the interacting scenario, we will utilize numerical methods to 
analyze the behavior of time-dependent properties and fractional energy density as a result 
of spatial curvature and initial conditions.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate the stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and applied evolutionary models such as Gaia DR2 and VSOP. This new study offers valuable data for various research areas such as stellar structure, stellar dynamics, and stellar activity, presenting four meaningful research findings: 1) analysis

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. A subsequent evaluation using German Chaos Computer Club's TRNG evaluation hardware and software toolkit showed that TuRaN surpasses state-of-the-art SRAM-based TRNGs in terms of throughput, achieves comparable energy consumption and latency performance, and is capable of generating randomly distributed 160-bit binary sequences at a rate of 12.1 Gigabits per second.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in a particular model known as the two-phase model.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.
