Additionally, this paper presents an evaluation of this new backend, comparing it to existing, closed-source backends. Despite the new backend's simpler implementation, it achieves similar performance to leading commercial compilers. This paper also examines how the new backend's efficiency could be improved using parallel processing techniques.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the second method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. In this model, a type of long-range interaction is investigated, focusing on two instances: an electron-muon pair produced in a radioactive decay, and a muon-tau pair generated through high-energy cosmic rays. Long-lived particles resulting from these interactions could have considerable propagation distances between their points of origin and disappearance, which in turn could influence the muon's lifetime as well as an anticipated drop in high-energy cosmic muon flux as it approaches the horizon. Current limits from searches for long-lived particles, as outlined in particle physics literature, may also be examined in light of the model's parameters.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper builds upon a broad framework for information quantification by leveraging measure theory, enabling the use of non-discrete probability distributions. We explore how to apply Shannon entropy and mutual information within this framework, and in doing so, we establish a natural connection with the concept of directed information, previously independently discovered. We then demonstrate several key properties among quantities defined through directed information. Furthermore, we clarify the relationship between common definitions of conditional mutual information and show that one definition is essentially equivalent to directed information. We then examine residual information, a novel concept, and investigate its relationship with conditional mutual information. We reveal that residual information is always non-negative and demonstrate that it equals zero for Gaussian distributions. We then discuss its potential applications and possible extensions to other information quantification methods.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to inflows and outflows. Employing a Lagrangian perspective, we establish that solutions exist and are unique and define a notion of weak solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the flow is continuous with respect to time, and also with respect to the initial condition. However, due to generally non-differentiable velocities, these refined regularity results only hold under carefully constructed semi-norms adapted from the standard norm. In general, the solution is not continuous with respect to any standard norm on the space of measures.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on the device hosting them. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by developing a method that allows a classifier to train and deploy a more efficient model, which can run on resource-constrained devices and provide accurate performance, despite being trained on limited data. The efficiency of this method is later proven through the comparison with traditional classifier-training methods.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it will have a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. For solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank, a Schreier growth gap of exp(n) applies unless they are virtually nilpotent, a criterion which also applies to solvable groups linear over ℚ. Lastly, a wide range of torsion-free solvable groups have a Schreier growth gap of n^2, a group type that also includes those linear over ℚ.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models and improve our understanding of the underlying physics. Furthermore, it's shown that the assumption of massless objects is incorrect and that using the mass underulates the complexity of the model, thus leading to inaccurate simulation results. Lastly, this work proposes several potential solutions to the problems encountered, including the development of customized discrepancy models that incorporate uncertainty and regularized optimization formulations that balance model simplicity and accuracy.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits that extend well beyond previous search findings in various scenarios.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and devised an optimization technique to achieve high efficiency in single-photon sources. This method incorporates a taper section to smoothly bridge the mode mismatch between the cavity and the nanobeam, ultimately enhancing the Purcell factor and source efficiency. Furthermore, we observed the resilience of our design in the face of real-world fabrication imperfections affecting hole variation in the taper-nanobeam system.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction, $\omega^4$, particularly in the low-frequency regime.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods like sector decomposition and 
are then translated into physical scenarios with a series solution, providing 
precision of at least eight digits. This method has an integrated accuracy 
checker and is shown to work with challenging examples like self-energy and 
vertex integrals and two-loop box integrals.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete, even when using limited binary valuations. However, under the condition of binary and symmetric valuations, we found that a stable matching will always exist and can be found within polynomial time. Additionally, we looked at finding the best stable matches that maximise total happiness when using binary and symmetric valuations. While finding the absolute optimum is a complex problem, we identified a more practical solution for approximating it closely.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall responses.
However, this equivalence does not apply when the coupling involves position-dependent
velocity of electrons. The presence of a significant valley Hall effect near a
neutral charge condition in the isotropic scenario mirrors that seen with changes
in bond lengths, while in the anisotropic scenario, geometric transport of valleys
is diminished similar to what is seen with deformation potentials.
Additionally, introducing strain variations leads to total inhibition of valley Hall
transport even when accounting for the dynamic behavior of these strains. The use
of a gate voltage allows for control over the direction of valley transport, thus
potentially utilizing valley Hall effect in 2D materials for vortechnology and
spintronic devices.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously established cloud completeness theorem.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a wide frequency range. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the minimal fault detection problem into a decoding challenge for such codes by treating the noise process as an adversarial strategy. We employ a reinforcement learning framework to educate agents that can decode surface codes effectively, including situations where the noise process is previously unknown. Multiple reinforcement learning agents are shown to outperform existing fault detection methods, with some generalizing well across various noise environments. We also explore the potential for these agents to learn noise profiles, leading to the discovery of multiple noise types that can be effectively countered by a single trained agent.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations.

Deep neural networks optimize well when given a head start, but it's unclear what representations are rich enough to kick-start optimal performance, especially when little data is available. By testing various initialization methods, we found that networks initialized with random special orthogonal matrices consistently outperformed those initialized with Glorot normalization, a common benchmark, and even exceeded the performance of networks initialized with accurate, but less flexible, matrix factorization representations. These results apply to multiple complex image classification tasks and demonstrate that SO(3) initialization provides a robust generalization across three distinct scenarios: when networks are overly flexible, when they lack sufficient data, or when they are simply looking for an optimal solution.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D heterostructures with an optimized single phase mask. We've verified the efficacy of our proposed approach with 120, 220, 450, and 600 grit ground glass diffusers, as well as with 323, 588, and 852 μm thick fresh chicken tissues including fluorescent properties. We've demonstrated the robustness of our proposed integrated system in controlling photon flow into and out of a localized fluorescent dye embedded in tissue. Detailed results reveal that our algorithm-driven integrated system achieves fast convergence and high image clarity with advanced resolution capabilities.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the existing literature reveal limitations under slower testing sample size growth. In contrast, the testing sample size requirement for DRITR is more relaxed than that of efficient policy evaluation using combined data. In Section 3, we emphasize the broad applicability and utility of DRITR.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, subsequently yielding significant gains in detection efficiency and spatial/temporal resolution.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at the speed of milliseconds.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, to showcase the benefits of this model, as evidenced by its similarity to the Hull-White one-factor model's Bermudan swaption prices on Bloomberg, and by its alignment with Bloomberg's constant maturity swap rates.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may be capable of discovering new parameters within reach, in which case a follow-up study at the far detector could achieve a decay width determination accurate to roughly 20-30 meV, although this would largely depend on the sterile neutrino mass, which the experiment cannot independently measure.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  This note outlines a method for conducting meta-analyses with clustered trials using both cluster-robust and hierarchical models.  Although robust estimators can mitigate small sample size issues related to usual estimators, they face a significant challenge when dealing with a limited number of clusters, which results in inaccurate assessments of variability and confidence intervals that are either too narrow or too wide.  This note suggests an alternative method based on a hierarchical model that is estimated using a Bayesian approach, drawing on the prior knowledge of correlations within and between clusters.  This approach can also be extended to accommodate additional predictors.  Utilizing simulated data and examining the performance of robust estimators, this note demonstrates that the proposed method can achieve more precise estimates and confidence intervals compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios with a limited number of clusters.  The suggested approach is implemented in the package lansing available on the CRAN repository.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results showing the transverse momentum broadening distribution in relation to rapidity and nuclear density are presented, along with a discussion of the significance of multiplicity in the production of a specific state and transverse momentum broadening.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of varying the relative densities of the liquids on the dynamics of the jet and the behavior of the air sheath.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal reprocessing costs. Our comprehensive evaluations, carried out across multiple test scenarios and algorithms such as an iterative solver and dense matrix multiplication, have consistently yielded a remarkably low overhead, at most 8.2 percent in some instances, with most experiments averaging under 3 percent, thereby making this approach an attractive solution for ensuring fault-tolerant HPC applications.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. Both findings support the flux-based three-body statistical framework, and our measurements of absorptivity and lifetime distributions provide valuable resources for further testing and validation of statistical models.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The study found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than that of J/$\psi$ mesons over the entire examined momentum range.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region, under the assumption of circular symmetry. Analysis of the synchrotron radiation suggests an average polarization level of $\sim 2.5$%, while the forward shock region indicates a nearly 5% polarization. Our model considers both thermal and non-thermal radiation contributions using detailed Chandra data for a spatial-spectral analysis. Our individual pixel search revealed several tentative polarization detections at $\sim 3\sigma$ confidence, indicating considerable turbulence in smaller regions than our current angular resolution allows. Our observations of Cas A indicate that X-ray emission within a radius of $\lesssim 10^{17}$ cm of the forward- and reverse shock regions primarily stems from synchrotron radiation. Our findings show that the X-ray emission from these regions exhibits considerable gradient, indicating a complicated history of jets and a complex internal structure in a high-energy source influenced by jet interaction with the remnant shell.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are highly uncertain due to their dependence on unknown quantum chromodynamic physics at high densities. As a result, the sound velocity in such matter also remains unknown. In density regions where binary nature of the equation of state holds, as indicated by the presence of two-phase dense matter, we find the lower limit of sound velocity to be less than the Loeb-Friedman limit, specifically around 0.4 in certain cases, indicating sub-relativistic behavior at high densities. Additionally, the gravitational wave emission from binary neutron stars in such scenarios is also reduced, making it around 30-40 percent lesser compared to the standard scenario.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

During gas-liquid interfaces in porous media, the liquid's molecular structure forms complex patterns.
These patterns create challenges for numerical simulations, as they require intricate representation and
high spatial resolution, which can be costly.
Our approach involves developing a new protocol to generate these patterns using simplified models, 
so we can focus computational resources on other aspects.
The core of our method is " skeletonization," where we refine existing templates by adding branching structures.
Our protocol is versatile and can be applied to various situations, as well as elements that affect interface growth,
like surface tensions and interface energies.
We demonstrate its effectiveness in three different scenarios, each with unique challenges.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the virus exhibits enzymatic activity.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, researchers find that this can result in a new crystal structure, F$\bar{4}3$m. Novel materials, KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, exhibit no dynamic instability; the inversion symmetry disruption by dopants triggers an increase in the total pseudo-angular momentum, which gets localized in the anion sublattice due to the introduction of impurities. This gives rise to novel properties, such as the generation of circularly polarized light in the four-band model of these systems.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our findings reveal that, when the conventional approximation is surpassed, nonadiabatic Born effective charges become well defined in metals within a specific frequency range. We also observe that, unlike in insulators, the summation of nonadiabatic Born effective charges from sublattices in metals does not equal zero but rather correlates directly with the Drude weight. These conclusions were verified through calculations using density functional perturbation theory, as applied to aluminum, and to two doped compounds, electron-doped tin disulfide and strontium titanate.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Our analysis indicates that the random variations in momentum conservation, resulting from the interaction of the fluid's average speed with the fluid's grainy structure as described by the random walk of the Langevin equation, must be taken into consideration within this range. This is in line with the understanding that similar random variations in angular momentum and energy are already well-recognized as driving the fluid's irreversible thermal dissipation.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models have been explored. This contrasts with another phenomenon where a magnetoelectric interaction traps a charge equal to $\pm e/2$ upon exposure to a magnetic monopole, commonly referred to as the Witten effect. The time-reversal symmetry being explicitly violated, as in the case of a Zeeman field influencing the surface electrons, can allow a description of a topological insulator's electromagnetic response via the surface electrons undergoing a half-integer quantum Hall effect.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving a satisfactory classification rate of 0.88 within a dataset and 0.80 across different datasets.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Moreover, it is suggested that the de Sitter horizon associated with holographic dark energy acts as a complete absorber for static detectors, given its infinite redshift effect.
As a result, thermal radiation emitted from this future de Sitter horizon may be the source of dark vacuum energy.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonsmooth objective, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques alongside the proximal gradient steps results in a significantly improved convergence rate for specific nondegenerated nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems. Moreover, our algorithm is accompanied by a numerical study that includes optimizations regulated by $\ell_1$-norm and trace-norm.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research presents numerous examples and characteristics to illustrate the distinction between weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and weakly prime ideals. Additionally, we explore the properties of this new type of ideal in a commutative ring with specific conditions.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189.9/fb, collected using the SuperKEKB $e^-e^+$ collider. To identify these decays, the research involved reconstructing the full recoil B-meson within hadronic end products, after which the researchers computed total branching ratios by performing statistical fits on missing mass square and dipion mass in the candidate signal, determining the former to be $4.12 \pm 0.64 (stat.) \pm 1.16 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ and the latter as $1.77 \pm 0.23 (stat.) \pm 0.36 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$. These findings are primarily subject to systematic error due to nonresonant influences on B-meson decay patterns.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While countries like Japan have
introduced more cost-effective and accessible smartphone-based solutions for
automated road condition monitoring, many other countries continue to search for
efficient alternatives. To address these issues, this study contributes in
several key ways. Firstly, it examines the suitability of Japan's approach for
global implementation. Secondly, a substantial, multi-national smartphone-based
dataset consisting of 26,620 images is developed. Thirdly, a set of adaptable
models capable of detecting and classifying road damage in multiple countries is
proposed. Lastly, recommendations are provided for other countries seeking to
adopt successful strategies from their peers. The created dataset is available at
https://github.com/sekilab/RoadDamageDetector/.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space to facilitate this correspondence.  Additionally, it ensures temporal alignment using a normalized position estimator.  Once the correspondence is established, the learned demonstrations can be directly transferred and applied to the target domain, empowering imitation.  The approach is validated through experiments across a diverse range of complex domains.

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic effects in a cosmological setting with existing magnetic fields. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to 1000 years following the initial protostar formation. To represent the protostars and their magnetic field structures, we utilized a stiff equation of state instead of the conventional sink particle approach. Ten years after the initial protostar formation, we observed an amplification in magnetic field strength from picogauss to kilogauss in a region extending from the protostar to its interaction boundary with surrounding gas sheets. This amplification led to increased angular momentum transfer from the disk to the protostar and subsequently to its merger with a nearby protostar. However, in cases where the merging protostars were not closely spaced, their magnetic field amplification led to their splitting into individual objects. We noted that when the amplification of the magnetic field increased in these objects, their collapse accelerated due to increased mass loading from surrounding gas, leading to a final star mass double that of magnetically influenced counterparts. We predict a bimodal initial mass function of the first stars resulting from magnetic effects, with a cut-off at around 2 solar masses, with more massive stars forming

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. We establish a deduction calculus for each of these concepts, show how to create the smallest possible bases, and also examine redundancy with multiple association rules. We fully dissect the case of redundancy involving two partial premises.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism by 4.3 percent or 12.6 percentage points relative to those who did not receive treatment.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future court involvement within a year or two following the initial conviction and that this reduction in court involvement holds consistent across various types of crimes along with the offender's criminal history.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian algorithm has been created to constantly update the map estimate and the associated uncertainty metric with every new data point, allowing the process to take place in real-time.

This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the hypothesis that sequences exhibiting unusual behavior often share similarities in their underlying Hidden Markov Model representations. The process involves first training HMM models on individual time series segments to create a density function based on these models. The density functions are then clustered to detect anomalies across all time series, with the assumption that similar time series may produce overlapping HMM representations. The performance of this method is demonstrated on synthetic and real-world data sets, showcasing its effectiveness in identifying anomalies. Furthermore, the method has shown potential in detecting irregularities in EEG signal data when compared to known signal patterns.

This research delves into a multi-faceted approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. The evaluation revealed that a multi-modal system outperforms unimodal and bimodal approaches in both normal and adverse environments, with a notable enhancement of 15% accuracy under noise and lighting disruptions. Furthermore, a lower correlation of errors was observed when using deep learning features on the auditory and visual datasets, indicating that deep models are better at filtering out irrelevant information. The source code and datasets are available for public access at our GitHub repository.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to create new instances. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective in boosting the performance of pre-optimized Transformer and Conformer models. Specifically, enhancements of up to 2.83 WER and 6.87 WER are seen in the LibriSpeech-960h test sets, and even higher when models were combined with fusion. Moreover, results show that augmenting models of varying sizes produces the best outcomes when trained in sequence, starting with the largest model. We've also discovered that augmenting existing data can be effective even when pre-training methods like BERT are employed.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that overlapped with the areas of several millimeter dust continuum emission gaps.
We observed that CO column density could be linked to surface-density fluctuations or chemical alterations, while C$_2$H column density was tied to changes in the C/O ratio rather than surface density changes in the gas.
However, our models require the presence of a massive planet (with a mass greater than 0.2 times Jupiter's mass) to explain this degree of gas depression.
But such a finding conflicts with the constraints set by the dust emission patterns and the gas pressure profile as measured through gas kinematics.
Our modeling suggests that a reduction in local CO abundance is essential in explaining the observed CO structure and that this factor outweighs any potential effect of a planet on the gas surface density. 
This study forms part of a special issue on the Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series focusing on the MAPS program.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. Furthermore, we found that these structures' ages, when compared to their actual age spread, appear excessively large. It is also worth noting that these structures, while seemingly homogeneous, can exhibit identical characteristics if composed of randomly selected stars from separate clusters, indicating that these structures might be mere coincidences. These findings call for a cautious interpretation of these structures' significance and importance in understanding the star formation history of the Milky Way galaxy.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 85% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We publicly release the VICTOR implementation at https://github.com/stevejpapad/Visual-InCompatibility-Transformer.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects.
