It plays a pivotal role in optimizing their utility across various applications. The incorporation of radical quantum phenomena such as coherence, entanglement, and nonclassicality has enabled their application in real-world contexts. The theoretical framework of quantum resource theory categorizes quantum states into 'free' and'resource' sets. Operations associated with free states emerge naturally from the system's constraints, whereas resource theories aim to discover and harness the potential within the restricted set. Recent breakthroughs in the field of standard harmonic oscillator quantum states have sparked rapid growth and advancements in the generalized quantum optical framework. The incorporation of contemporary ideas such as nonlinearity, non-Hermitian theories, and $q$-deformed bosonic systems aims to achieve elevated objectives in the field of quantum information. This article reviews recent developments in the resource theories of generalized quantum optical states and their applications in the realm of quantum information.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately determines the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments.

The main challenge hindering gallium nitride's performance as a high-speed transistor material lies in its lack of perfect matching to the lattice of other nitride materials. Researchers have made progress in growing gallium nitride on a patterned substrate, but its strain properties remain unclear. A recent study used advanced computational tools to investigate the uniaxial compression in gallium nitride when matched to six different nitride materials. The calculations showed that compressive strain in gallium nitride can shift the holes' energy bands to lower levels, creating better matching conditions with certain nitride materials, such as silicon carbide and aluminum gallium nitride. The findings also indicated that gallium nitride grown on patterned substrates exhibits either tensile or compressive strain, depending on the specific material it is matched to. Furthermore, the study revealed that compressive strain in gallium nitride can be combined with a small cobalt doping to create a desired flat band condition, resulting in improved material properties that could enhance the performance of gallium nitride-based high-speed transistors.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations, and establish a relationship between their Hopf differentials. Furthermore, we explore how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and discuss their behavior in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on the limiting object of nonparametric estimates of $P$. Furthermore, it is shown that these findings are significant for various spectral analysis techniques for Markov transition operators. Our study also provides a novel asymptotic perspective on the kernel conditional mean embedding, which underpins numerous techniques in kernel-based nonparametric inference.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide a formula reminiscent of the Dobinski-like formula.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for handling temporal information. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings, and leverages the notion of temporal scope to incorporate time-related information. We evaluate our approach on two datasets, and show that on one, it surpasses a leading baseline by 114%, while on another, it actually underperforms by 12%. Despite these varying results, our method has several attractive features, including the ability to avoid model selection and reduce the required computational resources.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores insplits and outsplits as key examples of strong shift equivalences, demonstrating that these equivalences lead to Morita equivalences that maintain consistency across various weighted gauge actions. Consequently, a question is raised about whether strong shift equivalence can be expressed as a product of insplits and outsplits.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and in strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first discovered high dimensional expanders.

Incorporating our methods also reveals a novel sparsification algorithm for high dimensional expanders, maintaining its key local spectral characteristics, offering an area of independent interest.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, things become more intricate as regular submodules are categorized by a flag variety, resulting in an abundance of choices that involve continuous parameters. Despite these complications, our analysis in select examples highlights how Hida theory and eigencurve geometry can facilitate the identification of a limited set of choices that possess notable arithmetic and'mixed-motivic' significance.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to leverage the atoms' sensitivity while minimizing the impact of noise 
without requiring the resolution of complex mathematical equations. In a key 
test, our Rydberg-deep learning system has enabled the direct extraction of 
encoded information from frequency-division multiplexed (FDM) signals, marking 
an important breakthrough in this field, and holding the potential to 
revolutionize the sensing and communication capabilities of Rydberg-based MW 
technology.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide a potential explanation for this phenomenon, as well as the absence of significant star formation elsewhere in the galaxy's disk.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that the atmospheric background temperature plays in the propagation of GWs. Data obtained from past missions including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, in combination with the new MAVEN findings, reveal an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the atmospheric background temperature, primarily found in the ODY mission's data collected over polar regions, rather than in the MGS and MRO datasets. Conversely, MRO's observations of the upper Martian atmosphere's behavior exhibit an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the Brunt-V\"{a}is\"{a}l\"{a} frequency. It is found that, in the atmospheric layer extending between 100 and 120~km in altitude, GW-induced density disturbances no longer correlate with temperature, instead aligning with atmospheric stability and pressure.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent experiments examining the forward J/psi production in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector are featured.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce visually relevant high-fidelity sounds and generate these in under the time it takes for audio playback on a high-end graphics processing unit. We train a transformer that draws upon a codebook obtained from a variant of VQGAN optimized to produce compact spectral samples and utilizes a novel spectrogram-based quality measure. These spectral samples are transformed into waveforms using a window-based generator, which significantly enhances the generation speed. Since there are limited tools for automatically assessing the quality of synthesized soundscapes, we introduce FID and MKL, a family of metrics relying on Melception, a novel audio classification model designed to evaluate the authenticity and relevance of synthesized soundscapes. Our results showcase the efficacy of this new method in both small-scale and large-scale datasets and reveal a notable enhancement in audio quality, file size, and processing time. A demo, the codebase, and generated samples are available at v-iashin.github.io/SpecVQGAN.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our IPO studio software.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently calculate the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbors classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming prior methods by several orders of magnitude, as supported by our system's experiments and benchmarks.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 megapascals, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as Mn$_3$Sn transitions into the helical state, its magnetization drops to nearly zero. The investigation of the material's spin wave also reveals a notable decline in energy at certain wave vectors when subjected to pressure. The findings suggest that Mn$_3$Sn exhibits a unique type of AHE, where the material's anomalous Hall resistance displays an unusual sublinear pressure dependence. The observed phenomenon is unlike any other AHE in similar materials and represents a rare occurrence where the AHE resistance does not scale directly with the material's magnetization or curie temperature.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as the
prevalent approach for RE. In particular, the reliability of DNNs in the RE task has
been verified through the evaluation of their robust performance in multi-task
scenarios, even with limited training data. This chapter serves as an introduction
to RE and DNNs in the RE context, followed by an exploration of the emerging trend
of using external knowledge to enhance RE. Moreover, the benefits of combining RE
with other pertinent NLP tasks, such as entity recognition and coreference resolution,
are also highlighted.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better understand this phenomenon, we explore its occurrence in two domains - social networks and relational learning datasets. Through our analysis, we reveal that this graph-hypergraph graph projection issue common among social networks differs from the underlying structure of relational learning datasets, which often involve multiplicity properties. Building on previous work, we develop and apply a new approach using hypergraph metrics to study this projection issue in social networks. In contrast, we find that current hypergraph metrics are inadequate for understanding multiplicity properties in relational learning datasets, and therefore, we introduce a new metric that effectively captures these properties. By using our new approach and metric, we gain deeper insights into hypergraph structures, projection characteristics, and multiplicity properties, ultimately contributing to the development of more accurate graph representation learning techniques.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies.
Current medical image analysis systems lack the knowledge of anatomical structure
appearance due to difficulty in collecting annotated data, thus restricting their
capability to narrow expertise areas, like diagnosing specific conditions. Our
research addresses this gap by incorporating human anatomy and allowing the
connection between report content and corresponding image content. To utilize
anatomical information, we introduce an advanced system to gather and integrate
human body structures from CT scans and incorporate it into PAXRay. The latter is
a comprehensive dataset for X-Ray anatomical structure segmentation. Our results
show that employing anatomical information significantly enhances visually linking
radiologists' observations with images, as our segmentations result in a 50%
better grounding outcome on the OpenI dataset compared to commonly used region
proposal methods. The PAXRay dataset is accessible at https://constantinseibold.
github.io/paxray/.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby not refuting the efficient market hypothesis.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which simplifies large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we represent the large deviation large scale limit of the KPZ equation as a periodic KPZ equation. The periodic KPZ equation is reformulated as the periodic Kardar--Parisi--Z equation through a variable transformation. The periodic Kardar--Parisi--Z equation is then mapped to a solvable integrable system based on the integration manifold concept. The exact solutions obtained allow for the calculation of hydrodynamic coefficients and the verification of predictions made by another theoretical approach. The solutions further enable us to derive exact large deviation functional results for one-dimensional active particle models, specifically the HPDP and the Langer--Sigg model.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the Hall effect. These theories are substantiated through the examination of associated electric field data.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on stratified flows is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to AI2-THOR evaluations. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including unseen indoor spaces and continuous real-world settings.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for ultralight axion dark matter. Our theoretical framework suggests that these black holes could be discovered by future gravitational wave experiments, specifically in experiments like LISA and the fifth generation of ground-based detectors, assuming they merge before z=2.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$. The measured branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ are potentially within reach for the BESIII and LHCb Collaborations. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ decay can also be used to determine the hadronic matrix element $X(3872)\rightarrow \psi(2S)\pi$, which could aid in understanding the nature of the $X(3872)$ resonance.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. In cases of defects, this shift occurs along closed paths in real space, with both instances characterized by non-trivial spin connections. This approach is utilized to determine the spin connections of three-dimensional Topological Insulators containing topological defects. The edge dislocation on the surface of a Topological Insulator generates a spin connection controlled by torsion, allowing electrons to move in confined circular areas and two-dimensional regions. The edge dislocations break parity symmetry, producing a current measured by the in-plane spin component on the surface, with this current accompanied by a tunneling density of states calculation for edge dislocations.
